source.title: Toward ethical cognitive architectures for the development of artificial moral agents

confidence_rationale: Converges independently on ARC-043's central structural commitment -- that ethics is derived from lower cognitive layers rather than implemented as a separate ethics module -- and proposes a layering (perception/world model -> social cognition and theory of mind -> moral emotion -> moral judgment) whose middle and upper portions align closely with ARC-043's Layers 2-5. Capped at 0.62 because it is a position/review paper making an argument rather than reporting a result: convergent theoretical judgement, not evidence, and two theorists agreeing on an architecture is weaker than it feels.
failure_signatures: The review identifies the ethical cognitive architecture as an open challenge rather than an achieved design -- no surveyed architecture (Soar, LIDA, ACT-R, iCub) actually implements the proposed layering, so the ordering is a research proposal on both sides of the comparison and neither side is independently confirmed.

The proposed stack places moral emotion between social cognition and moral judgment, whereas ARC-043 places shared valence (Layer 4) between shared world (Layer 3) and ethics (Layer 5) but derives the whole from epistemic ground upward -- the two orderings agree on direction but not on which primitives sit at the bottom, so the convergence is partial.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Ethical behaviour in artificial agents should be achieved by extending cognitive architectures with the mechanisms moral decision-making requires, rather than by adding an ethics module: moral agency is presented as depending on foundational cognitive functions (perception, world modelling), then social-cognitive capacities (mental-state reasoning, the ability to take another's perspective), then moral-emotion mechanisms acting as regulators of ethical decision-making, with moral judgment emerging from the integration of those layers rather than from ethical rules alone.
mapping.ree_translation: This is independent theoretical convergence on ARC-043's two structural commitments. First, that ethics is DERIVED (Layer 5 from Layers 0-4) rather than modular -- which is the same position REE holds under INV-001, that there is no explicit ethics module. Second, on the ordering itself: the review's sequence of world model -> theory of mind -> affective regulation -> moral judgment maps recognisably onto ARC-043's Layers 1/3 -> Layer 2 -> Layer 4 -> Layer 5, reached by authors with no exposure to REE.
mapping.mapping_caveat: This is a position paper arguing for an architecture, not a study demonstrating one -- the review's own conclusion is that ethical cognitive architectures are a set of unsolved challenges, and it reports that none of the surveyed architectures (Soar, LIDA, ACT-R, iCub) implements the layering it proposes. So both ARC-043 and this paper are proposals, and their agreement is convergent theoretical judgement rather than mutual confirmation; two architectures agreeing is not one architecture verified. The alignment is also partial: the review bottoms out at perception and world modelling and does not posit anything answering to ARC-043's Layer 0 (epistemic ground) or Layer 1 (existence), and it says nothing about ARC-043's Layers 6-9 -- the decision system under uncertainty and the action-consequence-learning closure.
mapping.source_context: Review and position paper in machine ethics / cognitive systems, surveying general cognitive architectures (Soar, LIDA, ACT-R, iCub) against the requirements of artificial moral agency; no implementation or empirical data.

confidence_components.notes: source_quality reflects a peer-reviewed but non-empirical position paper. transfer_risk is low because the source is already reasoning about artificial agents rather than requiring a biology-to-machine transfer -- this is the one entry in this pull for which the domains match natively. mapping_fidelity is the highest of the ARC-043 set because the source is arguing about layer ordering directly, which is what the claim asserts.
